strengths: The paper identifies a useful distinction between raw model inputs and interpretable explanatory variables, explaining why omitted macro-level factors can introduce confounding even when predictions are deterministic. This has a clear audience in interpretability, causal discovery, and model auditing.

Applying FCI with the background constraint that predictions cannot cause image content is a sensible use of established causal discovery tools. Under the stated assumptions, PAGs appropriately preserve uncertainty about causation and latent confounding.

The manuscript generally communicates its conceptual framework clearly. The synthetic example, two annotated-image applications, and discussion of feature selection and limited identifiability make the proposal concrete. A new algorithm or state-of-the-art predictive performance is unnecessary for this contribution to be useful.
weaknesses: Necessary: Sections 6.3–6.4 and Figures 9–10 overinterpret the graph summaries. Figure 8 pools definite-cause edges with possible-cause edges, although the latter remain compatible with pure confounding. Bootstrap frequency is therefore not a probability of causal relevance. Moreover, absence of an edge into the prediction does not exclude an indirect causal path through another feature. Report definite and ambiguous relations separately and use ancestry information from the full PAG, or narrow the claims about which features are causal or irrelevant.

Necessary: The X-ray sampling scheme creates an unresolved selection-bias problem. Controls are selected specifically for having 'no findings,' while cases are selected for pneumonia, so inclusion depends on disease status and explanatory findings. This can induce dependencies that latent-confounding allowance alone does not address, contrary to Section 3's dismissal of selection bias. Model or otherwise justify this sampling process, change the analysis population, or withdraw the causal interpretation of this application.

Necessary: The reliability of the conditional-independence tests is insufficiently established. With 240 X-rays and multilevel bird attributes conditioned on up to four other attributes, chi-square contingency tables can be extremely sparse. The manuscript provides no count diagnostics or explanation of sparse-table handling; bootstrapping does not repair miscalibrated tests. Specify the actual discovery samples and their relationship to model-training data, and provide evidence that the testing procedure supports the reported orientations.

Necessary: The Shapley counterexample requires correction. Appendix A.2 fixes the supposedly omitted variable at z3, leaving its value in the baseline and coalition evaluations; this is not the claimed backdoor adjustment using only Z2. In A.1, coalition evaluations also leave Z1's distribution unchanged when intervening on its parents Z2 or Z3. Define the intended attribution estimand and rederive the comparison before using it as evidence against confounding-unaware explanations.

Necessary: The simulation does not fully establish its asserted causal ground truth at the image level. Restricting the final hard classification to detected horizontal and vertical bars does not establish dependence only on their true presence: the shared image encoder can respond to other shapes, and Appendix B reports imperfect horizontal-bar detection. Verify the claimed invariance through controlled image interventions, or qualify the simulation as an approximate illustration.

Optional: Broader simulations across sample sizes and a comparison using the same macro-level annotations would help isolate the benefit of modeling latent confounding. The selected LIME and SHAP visualizations mainly illustrate differences in representation and explanatory goals.
